data.title: Civics students say one of the biggest obstacles is sitting in the next seat
data.description:
States across the country are adding civics requirements. 

Iowa’s new law makes passing a test drawn from the naturalization exam a condition of graduation starting this fall. Kentucky’s 2024 law, now in effect, requires a civic literacy course or a 100-question civics test. Alaska wrote civics into the diploma in June. Mississippi passed a law in April that folds civics into required coursework starting in 2027. 

The District of Columbia’s own requirement takes a different form. Its social studies standards, in effect since 2024, name “engaging in civil discourse and taking informed action” as a core practice, and its required government and civics course ends in an advocacy capstone: “Analyze the origins of a public policy issue, and present a proposal defending a position or invoking a call to action at the local, state or national level.”

These requirements strengthen civic knowledge and, in some cases, civic practice. A survey by my organization, the Sandra Day O’Connor Institute, points to a question that formal requirements cannot answer on their own: whether students will actually enter a disagreement.

This summer, we surveyed recent high school graduates who had attended school in 25 states and Washington, D.C., about how their civics classes handled disagreement. Fifty-eight percent said they had self-censored rather than say what they really thought about a political or civic topic because they were concerned about how others might react.

These were not, for the most part, students describing hostile classrooms. Seventy-three percent said they generally felt comfortable sharing honest views. Yet 51 percent of that comfortable group had still self-censored at least once, which suggests the silence was often situational. A room can be open in general and closed on a particular question. 

One student who attended high school in Washington, D.C. described “the lack of the comfortable space to talk about those things” when contested topics came up and said that was “why people would want to refrain from saying anything.”

The most striking finding was about whom they were worried about. Among students who self-censored, 91 percent cited classmates as a concern. Forty-one percent cited the teacher. That reorders a familiar debate that often turns on adults: teachers, administrators, parents, legislators. The students were pointing at the desks around them.

A similar reluctance appears among young adults more broadly: in Harvard’s Fall 2025 Youth Poll, 47 percent of Americans ages 18 to 29 said they avoided political conversations because they worried about how others would react.

Why does self-censoring matter? Because civic education has two related tasks. Students need to know how the American government works, and they need to practice what citizenship asks of them: forming a view, explaining it, hearing an opposing argument and working through the disagreement.

But an opinion withheld because speaking seems socially costly never gets tested against evidence or against a classmate’s objection, and the student loses a chance to practice the part of citizenship that happens among other people.

Teachers remain central because they help shape the conditions in which peer pressure operates. Fifty-three percent of respondents in our survey had at least sometimes seen a teacher avoid, cut short or shut down a political or current-events discussion. In our 2025 survey of civics teachers, nearly 80 percent said they had self-censored or avoided certain topics because they feared pushback or controversy. These findings suggest caution on both sides of classroom discussion.

The research the report cites helps explain why classmates loom so large. One study of 10th grade social studies classes built around controversial issues found that students’ perceptions of their peers influenced participation more than the teacher’s behavior did. Other research finds that students can misread those peer norms. What they assume classmates think and what classmates actually think do not always match.

The report’s recommendations can be carried out inside any classroom, including Washington D.C.’s capstone course. Ask students, anonymously, whether a classmate who voices an unpopular opinion should still be treated with respect, and whether they think most classmates agree. Ask where students support the norm but assume their peers do not. Sharing the results may help correct the misperception. Let students argue an assigned position, or submit an opening response without a name attached, before they are asked to speak for themselves. 

Because 26 percent of those who self-censored worried about being discussed or posted about on social media, make it an expectation that classmates’ remarks are not recorded, posted or circulated out of context. And train teachers in the peer dynamics of a discussion, not only its technique: when to protect a minority view, and when to step in.

A civics test can confirm that a graduate knows the three branches of government. It cannot confirm that she will defend an unpopular view to a classmate and still be on speaking terms afterward. Our survey suggests that willingness cannot be taken for granted.

Liam Julian is chief of programs and public policy at the Sandra Day O’Connor Institute, a nonpartisan nonprofit founded by Justice Sandra Day O’Connor. The Institute’s new report, “Why Are Students Self-Censoring in Civics Class?,” is available at oconnorinstitute.org/research2026.

data.title: Department of State approves potential $2.6 billion military air defense equipment sale to Ukraine
data.description:
The State Department approved a potential $2.6 billion air defense equipment sale to Ukraine Friday as its conflict with Russia resumed following trilateral talks with U.S. special envoys. 

In a congressional notification, the State Department wrote that the Ukrainian government requested S-300 Clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, counter-drone radars and other related elements of logistics and program support.

The department continued that “if the proposed purchase is concluded, Ukraine would finance it using a combination of European contributions and U.S. Foreign Military Financing appropriated during the prior Administration.”

“The FMF [Foreign Military Sale] will be counted as a U.S. capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund via a 1:1 reimbursement,” the agency stated. 

The U.S. Embassy in Kyiv similarly posted on social media that the potential sale would “improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats” by “equipping it to conduct self-defense and regional security missions with a more robust air defense capability.”

President Trump also signed the Russia sanctions into effect Friday, which authorizes further sanctions and tariffs against Russia.

The bill — championed and named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) — called for the president to calls for the president to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the top five purchasers of Russian energy, or on countries helping Russia evade sanctions — even extending current sanctions on Iran

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the Russia sanctions bill “critically important” for his country.

“The best way to honor Lindsey’s memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly,” Zelensky said. “And the best reward for everyone helping us put pressure on Russia to end its war will be peace.”

The actions follow attempted trilateral peace talks between Moscow, Kyiv and U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law. Witkoff said the U.S. is confident that talks will result in a “good resolution” to the conflict after a weekend-long ceasefire was called for their visit. 

The conflict, however, has reignited since peace talks, with Russia launching strikes against targets in Kyiv and other major cities earlier this week, according to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry. European Union Ambassador to Ukraine Katarina Mathernova confirmed that at least two people were killed and 10 injured in the strikes.

Zelensky, speaking at a press conference, said his country had pleaded to the U.S. and other allies to provide critical air defenses — particularly Patriot interceptors — to counter Russian ballistic missiles before the winter.

data.title: Beware of politicians claiming to protect us from the press
data.description:
This week, it became apparent that everyone believes in a free press, as long as it costs them nothing.

Politicians in both parties are now using their offices to insulate themselves from opposing coverage — all in the name of protecting the public or the press.

President Trump has ordered the banning of critical media companies from the White House. Meanwhile, Democrats are fighting to block a corporate media merger on equally raw political grounds.

At the White House this week, President Trump declared, “I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW … and Politico.” He then added that he did not understand why the courts allow the media to print “fake news,” raising the possible addition of censorship to banishment.

On Capitol Hill and across the country, Democrats were pursuing their own political litmus test for media. Twelve blue states are in court seeking to block the acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance. While framing their claims in dubious antitrust terms, many admit that they are trying to protect one of the very companies banned by Trump as a liberal platform: CNN.

Previously, Democrats shut down the government in part over a decision to withdraw government subsidies for another liberal news outlet, National Public Radio. Years ago, some Democrats even asked cable companies to consider dropping Fox News.

Both Trump and the Democrats are oblivious to the implications of their actions, blinded by the political costs of a free press and a free market.

There is little recognition, let alone remorse, among these politicians. For Trump, many in the public rallied to his side in condemnation of media bias during the last election. I have joined in the criticism of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico for their coverage. But this ban is a frontal assault on the free press itself, shattering long-standing principles maintained by past presidents.

Presidents have long condemned the media. George Washington referred to them as those “infamous scribblers.” Thomas Jefferson complained that “Nothing can now be believed which is seen in a newspaper. Truth itself becomes suspicious by being put into that polluted vehicle.” Yet they recognized that their oath to uphold the Constitution included a sacred duty to preserve and protect the free press.

For the Democrats, the opposition to the merger is equally transparent. Figures such as former Obama administration official Norm Eisen have opposed the Warner Bros.-Paramount merger as an attack on democracy itself. Their aim is to prevent the conservative David Ellison, chairman of Paramount Skydance, from gaining control of CNN as well as existing media assets such as CBS. Despite using antitrust law, he and others have made it plain that their aim is to preserve CNN and other outlets as liberal allies.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) declared that it is a power grab by the “oligarchs,” and that Ellison gaining control of CNN is “not acceptable. This merger must be opposed.”

Former Obama adviser Dan Pfeiffer called on Democrats to stop the merger to prevent an effort to “make CNN more MAGA-friendly.”

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) has warned that allowing the merger will “subvert CNN’s editorial independence.”

Notably, while MS NOW, CNN, and many of these individuals are condemning Trump’s announcement, they have eagerly joined the movement to block a lawful merger on political grounds. Others have pitched a deal where the merger can go through, but that they want CNN as “a strong consolation prize,” presumably to be sold to a liberal owner.

Again, there is little thought of the costs. There rarely is. When Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and others took credit for blocking the merger of Spirit Airlines with JetBlue, they declared it a victory for the Biden administration and the Democrats. Spirit Airlines then went bankrupt and all of its employees were fired.

In this case, CNN may be the Spirit Airlines of the media. It has been struggling with both revenues and ratings, despite occasional spikes. While the Democrats want to preserve the liberal platform that regularly features their interviews and narratives, CNN often operates dangerously to the baseline on the key advertising demographic needed to keep the lights on.

Warner Bros. has lost billions. The merger would be good for both companies and their employees. Under the guise of opposing a monopoly, Democrats are opposing a deal that has been cleared by the European Commission and once-skeptical experts.

I have worked for four networks as a legal analyst for 30 years, and I want CNN to flourish. We need strong media companies. That means that we need to support both the free press and the free market in maintaining journalistically and financially strong media companies. That often means setting aside our personal disagreements with coverage to oppose political manipulation of the media by either party.

I previously have written about the media and free speech in an “age of rage.” Presidents and politicians have periodically allowed their anger or interests to overwhelm their judgment. President John Adams declared, “The liberty of the press is essential to the security of the state.” Yet, his administration targeted reporters and writers under the infamous Alien and Sedition Acts.

Politicians are again using their power to manipulate the press by limiting their exposure to media criticism. They are seeking to control what the public reads and watches to protect us from “fake news” or “corporate messaging.”

For centuries, politicians have played on our anger or partisanship to target the media. To defend the free press and the free market is not to agree with these companies or their coverage. It is to defend our right to make our own decisions on what news to read and whom to believe.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.“

data.title: These were the hottest baby names 50 years ago. What happened?
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – There’s a good chance that if you’re turning 50 this year, your name is Jennifer or Michael or Jason. There’s also a pretty good chance that if you are a grandparent or will be soon, the newest member of your family will not have at least two of those names. 

The odds are relatively high that, instead, their name will be Liam or Olivia or one of the handful of others that have been incredibly popular in recent years. 

Before Liam and Olivia became the most popular baby names in the U.S., it was Michael and Jennifer at the top of their respective lists. A Nexstar review of data from the Social Security Administration shows that in 1976, Jennifer was the most popular name for newborn girls in every state, while Michael was the most popular for boys in 34 states. Jason claimed the top spot in 15 others, while James was No. 1 in two. 

The SSA reports that between 1926 and 2025, more than 1 million Jasons have been born, making it the No. 26 boy name overall across the time period. There have been more than 1.4 million Jennifers over the same span, making it the third-most-popular name for girls. 

They weren’t in the limelight forever, though. It’s been at least a decade since Jason even landed in the top 100 baby names for any state, and even longer for Jennifer. 

So what happened? 

It was those Jennifers and Jasons, and likely their friends, who helped break the trend. 

As Steph Coffield, a baby name advisor for BabyCenter, explains, Jason began losing popularity after “all of those Jasons became new dads.” 

“At that point, names that ended in  ‘-son’ started to explode in popularity — like Jackson, Mason, Bryson and others. They felt familiar since they had the same ending as ‘Jason,’ but distinct,” she explained.

Similarly, when Jennifers — or Jens or Jennies or whatever nickname they had to go by because of another Jennifer in their school or workplace — became moms, they, too, “wanted their children to have more distinctive names,” Coffield said. 

There’s another aspect, too. The popularity of Jennifer in the 1970s and 1980s is an example of a name that became “tied to that generation.” Colleen Slagen, the baby name consultant behind NamingBebe.com, explained that “by the time the next generation starts having kids, Jennifer feels like a ‘mom name.’”

There are some names that, despite how popular they may become, have never faded. That includes Michael and James, which Slagen described as “founding father” type names. They haven’t ranked outside the top 100 ever. James hasn’t even fallen out of the top 20. 

“These are timeless names with more stable popularity curves [versus] the steep peak we saw with Jennifer and Jason,” Slagen explained via email.

“I think that because names today are less saturated — that is, people are choosing from a wider pool and the popular names aren’t used with the same frequency that they were in past generations — we will see fewer ‘timestamped’ names,” Slagen said, noting, though, that some names may still fall into that category.  

We could be on the precipice of watching some popular names become “extinct.” Earlier this year, BabyCenter predicted several boy names ending in -y — Huxley, Grady and Harry, for example — are among those that could soon fade like Jason and Jennifer. Unique spellings of normal-sounding names, like Maddison and Alivia, may also be destined for history. 

Social media suggests Gen Z — some of whom are likely too young to have children — have already declared “Jessica” the newest iteration of “Karen,” potentially setting it up for extinction.

There may be a reason why names rapidly lose prevalence. Slagen told Nexstar in 2024 that she encourages people to avoid trendy names. 

“Any name that jumps over 100 spots a year in popularity … in my mind, that’s the sign of a name that’s going to go out of fashion,” she explained, adding that she suggests soon-to-be parents consult the Social Security Administration’s annual rankings of the top-used baby names in the country. 

If you want to know whether or not your name is extinct, you can use the Social Security Administration’s lookup tool, which can show how popular it was each year.

data.title: MS NOW says their journalists have been denied access to the White House
data.description:
The White House denied MS Now journalists access to its grounds Saturday, the network announced, a day after President Trump said he was banning the outlet, along with CNN and Politico, from the premises after accusing them of producing “purposefully negative stories.”

“Earlier this morning MS NOW journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS Now wrote in a statement Saturday morning. “MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”

MS Now correspondent Akayla Gardner said her press badge had been disabled when she arrived at the White House for work Saturday morning; Gardner delivered the report live from outside the grounds.

She said she that, while she cleared the initial allowed security checkpoint, White House personnel stopped her when she attempted to scan her badge to enter. <To avoid

“It did not work. There was a red beeping light,” Gardner said.

The MS Now reporter said an officer then took the badge and told her it had been disabled. When asked why, Gardner said the officer told her the decision was “above him.”

Her White House credentials were confiscated, but her producer badge was still active, Gardner added.

Trump announced his decision to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House “effective immediately” in a Friday Truth Social post, accusing the three outlets of reporting false information about him and his administration.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote, adding that additional news outlets could also be blocked.

Multiple free-speech groups and press organizations, including Fox News contributors, denounced the ban — arguing it violated these outlets’ constitutional right to press freedom.

MS Now, CNN and Politico all pushed back after Trump announced his ban, each issuing responses condemning the restrictions.

Trump has long feuded with CNN’s reporting, recently calling the network “crooked as hell” and “a very corrupt organization” in a June Oval Office conference. He also frequently criticizes one of its White House correspondents, Kaitlan Collins, who he described as a “corrupt reporter” with “hatred in her eyes” during the same meeting.

“Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right,” a CNN spokesperson said in a statement.

Trump also accused Politico of receiving $8 million in government subsidies for its “Politico Pro subscription,” something the outlet has denied.

“The claims that POLITICO received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked,” Politico said in a statement.

data.title: Live updates: Relationship with Canada still rocky ahead of UN General Assembly; AI companies hit with new lawsuit
data.description:
The tension between President Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has intensified since the Canadian leader’s visit with the European Union (EU) earlier this week. 

U.S. and Canada have continued to place tit-for-tat tariffs on American and Canadian goods. The relationship has also been stained this week by the European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen’s proposal to make Canada an associate member of the EU this week, which Trump said would be a “horrible act.”

This comes ahead of Trump’s scheduled appearance at the United Nations General Assembly next week, where international heads of state will gather in New York City as the U.S.’s war with Iran wages past the 200-day mark and Russia’s war with Ukraine escalates.

But there are currently no scheduled meetings between Carney, according to The Hill’s Mallory Wilson and Helen Huiskes.

On Friday, AI companies Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google were all included in a lawsuit alleging “collusion” between the tech giants.

Plaintiffs claim that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis made an illegal business agreement among competitors by agreeing to slow the development of their AI systems, violating U.S. antitrust law.

The lawsuit points to a recent proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who called for “industry-wide coordination” to “pace the frontier” of Ai development due to recent safeguard concerns.

President Trump is spending the day in Camp David Saturday after arriving late the night before, marking his third trip this year to the presidential retreat in Frederick County, Maryland.

The president is not slated to make any public appearances during his stay at the presidential retreat and will return to the White House on Sunday.

Follow live below.

data.title: Why is the Trump administration targeting  foreign journalists?
data.description:
For more than 40 years, a Reagan-era policy enabled foreign correspondents to stay in the U.S. lawfully as long as their job required. This summer, the Department of Homeland Security announced these journalists will face restrictive new visa requirements that could be abused to punish those critical of the Trump administration.  

The new rules would cap journalists’ initial admission to no more than 240 days (less than eight months), eliminating a flexible and welcoming policy that has lasted decades across both Republican and Democratic administrations.  

Although the U.S. has long been a champion of press freedom, the Trump administration has shown itself to be unabashedly antagonistic toward the media. The new policy disturbingly echoes those found in Russia, China and Iran, which use strict visa compliance rules to punish journalists and media outlets that report on their governments unfavorably. 

Across the government, agencies have taken extreme actions to arrest and charge journalists; issue subpoenas, including to journalists’ family members; shut down access to the White House and the Pentagon; threaten broadcasters; and sue news outlets. The most egregious acts have been tied to the immigration crackdown, including revoking visas, detaining and even deporting foreign journalists.

Taken together, this shows a pattern of hostility unlike any in modern U.S. history, one in which the federal government aims to pacify and impose its views on the free press and imperils the rights enshrined in the First Amendment.

For decades, the Reagan-era policy allowed journalists to work for multiple years, granting them the time and stability needed to build deep networks and trusted contacts, understand and report on American life, build expertise, lease a house, and enroll children in schools. With this flexible system, foreign journalists could broadcast a thorough and nuanced view of America’s story to their home audiences, in their own languages and cultural frames. 

Homeland Security claims, without substantiated evidence, that the new requirements are needed for “national security and fraud prevention.” Yet, by its own admission, the department recognized “the lack of public data cited in the proposed rule regarding fraud and overstays specific” to journalists.

For journalists seeking a longer stay, Homeland Security would compel them to put in an extension application every 240 days to remain in lawful status, incurring additional costs, giving new biometric data, and possibly needing to be interviewed about the content of their reporting. Such intrusive and expansive scrutiny risks granting the government the power to target foreign journalists in connection with their reporting. 

Before arriving in the U.S., foreign journalists undergo thorough security vetting and are interviewed by U.S. diplomats overseas. As such, the U.S. government holds comprehensive information about their resumes, their employers’ information and their purpose of travel. 

The new rule has sent chills among the foreign press community, fearing how the government could go after journalists for their reporting and suppress access to independent information. In this new milieu, foreign journalists are likely to second-guess their editorial decisions and self-censor to avoid running afoul of Homeland Security monitors.

In August, reflecting a profound concern for the right to a free press, the Committee to Protect Journalists and other press freedom advocates called on the U.S. Congress to exercise its power of oversight and to block the rule.

Congress must ensure that the ability of the foreign press to undertake continuous reporting is not obstructed through administrative artifice, recognizing that the Department of Homeland Security also faces a processing backlog and is affected by budgeting disputes and agency shutdowns. 

Thankfully, a federal judge intervened just before the regulations were set to go into effect, after unions and advocacy groups sued the government over the new rules. The judge, F. Dennis Saylor of Boston, said the amended policy was based on “exceptionally weak” rationales. “The weakness of the connection between the rule and its purported rationales,” he continues, “raises legitimate questions as to whether its real purpose is not to safeguard national security and protect our borders, but to achieve other, undisclosed, goals.” 

We should recall that when the Reagan administration adopted flexible and enabling rules for foreign journalists, the United States was championing individual rights and freedoms in its global contest against the now-defunct Soviet Union, which was notorious for repressing free and independent journalism. 

More than 40 years later, the Trump administration has turned its back on America’s proud commitment to liberty for all. Like Saylor, we must continue the fight for open inquiry, transparency and free expression. 

Loghman Fattahi is the U.S. advocacy representative at the Committee to Protect Journalists, an independent, nonprofit organization that promotes press freedom worldwide.

data.title: Lawsuit accuses Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, Google of AI pacing 'collusion'
data.description:
AI companies Anthropic, OpenAI, Space XAI and Google are being sued over alleged collusion as pressure mounts to slow the rapid development of AI.

The complaint, filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, points to a recent proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who called for “industry-wide coordination” to “pace the frontier” as concerns mount over the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI.

“We must slow the space in which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a Sept. 12 essay.

The plaintiffs allege that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis made an illegal business agreement among competitors by agreeing to slow the development of their AI systems, violating federal antitrust law.

Within hours of Amodei publishing his essay, Musk responded, saying “Dario is right,” while Altman also said he agreed with Amodei. Hassabis called the proposal “the right path forward,” according to the complaint.

Nick Rowley, one of the attorneys who filed the lawsuit on behalf of four plaintiffs, said decisions about AI safeguards should be made through government action rather than private agreements among major technology companies.

Rowley said in a statement to Politico that the case was filed to ensure “private self-serving agreements between the world’s most powerful ‘for profit’ technology companies” don’t result in AI “quickly spin[ing] out of human control.”

“Humanity deserves iron clad safeguards when it comes to extinction event threats such as nuclear warfare and now the biggest risk to mankind in history,” Rowley continued. “The rule of law should be established transparently and lawfully by our government, with accountability to the public.”

The plaintiffs include Florida attorneys Charles Buist and Nick Spetsas, Cheyenne Hunt — an attorney who played a key role in exposing the sexual misconduct allegations against former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.) — and California resident Christine Bullock.

Amodei’s proposal had already raised antitrust concerns among lawmakers in Washington, after the Anthropic CEO suggested the government could provide a “narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations” so AI companies could work together on standards without violating U.S. antitrust law.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) rejected the idea during a Senate hearing with FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday.

“There is absolutely no world in which I will consent to giving the most powerful companies in the history of the world — a small group of three or four of them — antitrust exemptions so they can what … collude together?” Hawley said. “Absolutely no way that’s happening.”

data.title: Healthy food is the missing piece in health savings and flexible spending accounts
data.description:
Our country is facing a chronic disease epidemic. Sixty percent of American adults have at least one chronic disease and we spend $5.3 trillion a year on healthcare.  

In a political climate where it’s hard to agree on anything, the positive in this case is that there has been a decades-long, widespread alignment that diet and exercise are critical to reversing this trend. As CEO of an organic food provider, I am glad to see things are changing in the right direction. 

So why haven’t we made more progress? As it relates to the food side of the equation, the release of the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s updated dietary guidelines has received a lot of attention, but every version of those guidelines for decades has lifted up the benefit of whole fruits and vegetables and for good reason. 

PLOS Medicine found in a 2019 study that if Americans met their daily fruit and vegetable guidelines, they could prevent 1.93 million cardiovascular events and save $40 billion in U.S. healthcare costs. An apple a day really could keep the emergency room away. Yet only 10 percent of Americans eat the recommended amount of vegetables and only 12 percent eat the recommended amount of fruit. 

This is not a consumer education problem. It’s an access problem. Tightening budgets and rising food costs shift hungry consumers to cheaper and more heavily processed foods.  

On the exercise front, in June, Harvard released a new study that found that long-term resistance training increased your chances of living longer, in fact it represented a 13 percent lower risk of all-cause mortality, 19 percent lower risk of cardiovascular mortality and 27 percent lower risk of neurological disease mortality.  

The percentages are startling, but we’ve known about the link between exercise for so long that our federal government has gone beyond simply encouraging us to go for a run. There’s a reason the IRS allows health savings accounts and flexible spending accounts to pay for exercise apps, gym memberships and equipment.

So why haven’t we made the same possible for healthy food? 

Americans have $160 billion sitting in health savings and flexible spending accounts — pre-tax money specifically earmarked for their health. Under IRS rules, they can spend it on exercise programs, prescription drugs, medical devices, acupuncture and even sunscreen.

But not on an apple. Not on a bag of spinach. Not on the organic blueberries that decades of research show can reduce the risk of heart disease, type two diabetes and certain cancers. On the contrary, a flexible spending account will allow an American family to pay for a type two diabetes drug, Metformin, but it won’t pay for the vegetables that could help someone avoid needing it.

This isn’t just ironic — it’s backwards.  

More than half of American adults — 119 million people — have high blood pressure and have to take blood pressure meds they pay for with their health savings accounts. But those same accounts won’t pay for the foods proven to lower blood pressure without drugs. 

We can fix this. 

We have over $160 billion in health savings account assets and roughly $30 billion in annual flexible spending account contributions, but the IRS definition of health excludes the single most evidence-backed intervention for chronic disease prevention: eating more fruits and vegetables. 

Congress should expand health savings and flexible spending account eligibility to include fresh, frozen and canned fruits and vegetables. Whole produce; not processed food disguised as health food. It takes pre-tax money that workers already earned and already saved for and lets them use it for the foods that prevent disease.  

Congress should amend health savings and flexible spending eligibility to include fruits and vegetables, to allow families to use $500-$1,000 a year of that money to buy healthy fresh food. And on the executive branch side, the Make America Healthy Again Commission should include health savings and flexible spending produce eligibility in its policy recommendations. 

Will this work? Well, we don’t have to look far to make a case. Two programs that empower families, SNAP and WIC, prove consumers will buy healthy food if they have access.  

The Double Up Food Bucks program operates in more than 25 states and provides a $1 for $1 match for SNAP eligible families to buy fresh fruits and vegetables. The WIC program provides participants with a monthly allowance specifically to purchase fresh, frozen and canned fruits and vegetables.  

Guess what happened? The National Institutes of Health found that the Double Up Food Bucks program led people to spend more on fruits and vegetables, buy greater variety, and make them a bigger part of their grocery purchase.

There is even a recent precedent for this. In March 2020, Congress passed the CARES Act, expanding flexible spending account eligibility to include over-the-counter medications. I’d argue fruits and vegetables are the ultimate over-the-counter medicine — good for you, proven to help and something we should make easier for people to afford.

Turning around the chronic disease trends in this country won’t happen overnight. But we can’t afford to leave proven solutions on the table.

It’s time for Congress to act.

Ricky Silver is CEO of organic food provider Daily Harvest.

data.title: Carney's Euro trip inflames Trump tensions
data.description:
The tension between President Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has only intensified amid the latter’s cozying up with the European Union (EU) on a high-profile trip this week. 

The relationship between the U.S. and Canada has been increasingly strained due to tit-for-tat tariffs on American and Canadian goods and Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” along with his repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st state.

Trump lashed out Wednesday against a proposal to make Canada an associate member of the EU, telling reporters it could be considered a “hostile act” and threatening to slap tariffs or stop trading with Europe if it goes ahead. 

The proposal, put forward by European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen, would be a new status for the bloc and has yet to be clearly defined. Leaders from both sides will meet in Montreal at the end of October, where the proposal to take the Canada-EU relationship to a higher level will likely be discussed in more detail. 

Carney welcomed the proposal in his appearance at the European Parliament on Thursday, although he specified he is not seeking full membership in the EU, but rather more integration in trade and defense to strengthen both Canada and the bloc. 

“We do not seek power to dominate others,” he said. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

The deterioration in relations between the U.S. and Canada is without precedent in what has long been an ironclad alliance. While Carney has touted a geopolitical realignment, he regularly says America remains a crucial partner. 

Still, the rift has already affected both countries, on an economic and social level, as Canadians rethink buying American products and visiting the US as tourists.

Imran Bayoumi, deputy director at the Atlantic Council, said the “volatility coming from the United States” and Canada’s desire to diversify partners explain the latest developments in Europe. 

“I think the Trump driver is the main one, but I think there’s also a recognition that it’s a more dangerous geopolitical world,” Bayoumi said. “Canadian foreign policy is still rooted in a values-based approach and I’m not sure it can be said that the U.S. has that same outlook right now, so I think trying to meet the EU on that same plane is important to Canadians.”

Some senators said Thursday that they’re not surprised Canada is looking elsewhere for allies amid the tension with Trump, but that the U.S.-Canada relationship should be preserved.

“It’s understandable to me that the EU and Canada would look for ways that they can start to build relationships,” Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) said. “You start to want to find new friends.”

Smith said her state is already seeing economic effects of fraying interchange with Canada, which is Minnesota’s largest export market. 

Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) said the same about his state. 

“We had a lot of Canadians that come across the border to go to restaurants and shop, they don’t do that now,” Peters said. “They’re like, ‘I’m not going to go across to America.’ So, it’s really sad, and for us too to have to deal with that. So hopefully, we’ll get through it. I think it’s a good friendship. It’ll last, but it’s certainly being strained.”

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said the EU membership idea is just both countries entertaining a way to hit back at the U.S. 

“They’re just trying to irritate the United States. They’re just sending a message that they know that Canada is not happy with us,” Rounds said of the EU. “I think it’s unfortunate that that happens, but it’s one more way in which Canada can express their hurt.” 

Rounds, too, said the Canadian relationship was important and that the whole back-and-forth should have a goal. 

“They’re our friends, they’re our allies, and I think the bottom line is, you need to get results at some point,” Rounds said of Canada. “Tariffs have a place, but the end result should be a better relationship when we’re all done.”

Trump told reporters Wednesday that Canada has “been a terrible trade partner” and that he doesn’t see them becoming an associate member of the EU.

“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things,” he said. “So, if they do that, if Europe does that, with a bad intention — if it’s a good intention, that’s fine — if it’s bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility.” 

Bayoumi said the U.S. “might not love it as a policy,” if Canada and the EU strike a deal.

“But at the same time, if that’s Washington’s position, there are actions that it could also take to start to repair the relationship with Canada,” he said.

Trade negotiations broke down last month between the U.S. and Canada after weeks-long negotiations. Both sides accused the other of adding stipulations last month that were nonstarters. The breakdown led to 50 percent tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods, with Ottawa then announcing dollar-for-dollar counter tariffs on U.S. goods.

The standstill is likely to continue into the fall. While both Trump and Carney are attending the United Nations General Assembly next week, there are no confirmed plans for the two to meet.

Even if things thaw, Carney has said there’s no going back to the previous status quo. 

Carney came into power on a wave of anti-American sentiment and has sought to realign Canada’s relationship to the world as a “middle power” that doesn’t need to rely on “hegemons,” as he described it in January.

“I think the relationship will be different regardless of who’s in power in 2028, regardless of what comes next,” Bayoumi said. “I think you’re going to have a Canada that’s more used to its autonomy, asserting itself, and hyper-focused on its national interest.”

“But I also think the bilateral relationship is going to endure,” he continued. “You can’t change geography, Canada, the U.S. share a land border, share a binational military command, they still have tons of shared interests, close economic ties and so those levels and areas of cooperation are going to persist regardless.”
